**Project summary:**
*Threads of Home* is a community textile archive and accompanying series of participatory workshops that will collect, document, and celebrate the diverse textile traditions present in Darebin's multicultural community. My practice as a textile artist centres on the idea that cloth carries memory. I work with found and donated textiles, often incorporating embroidery, patchwork, and natural dyeing techniques. For this residency, I propose to extend my practice outward — rather than creating a solo body of work, I will facilitate the creation of a community archive. I will photograph each object, record the owner's story (with their permission), and create a small embroidered response piece that will be displayed alongside the original object. The resulting archive will be both physical and digital, with the digital component hosted on the library's website.

I am particularly interested in the way that textile traditions are passed down through families and communities, and how these traditions adapt when people migrate to a new country. Darebin is home to significant communities from the Indian subcontinent, Southeast Asia, the Horn of Africa, and the Balkans, among others. 11:30 – Tea break. Informal chat. Several participants asked about the library's new opening hours – I didn’t have the updated info, so I said I’d check and bring it next week. (Follow-up: info sent via email to the group on 26 Feb.)

**Section 19: Project Proposal — Detailed Plan**

*Please provide a detailed outline of your proposed project, including your creative approach, timeline, and how the residency space would be used.*

**Project title:** *Threads of Home: A Community Textile Archive*

**Project summary:**
*Threads of Home* is a community textile archive and accompanying series of participatory workshops that will collect, document, and celebrate the diverse textile traditions present in Darebin's multicultural community. The project will culminate in a public exhibition in the library's community gallery space, featuring both the collected textile pieces and the stories of the people who made them.

**Creative approach:**
My practice as a textile artist centres on the idea that cloth carries memory. I work with found and donated textiles, often incorporating embroidery, patchwork, and natural dyeing techniques. For this residency, I propose to extend my practice outward — rather than creating a solo body of work, I will facilitate the creation of a community archive. Members of the public will be invited to bring a textile object of personal significance to one of our documentation sessions. I will photograph each object, record the owner's story (with their permission), and create a small embroidered response piece that will be displayed alongside the original object. The resulting archive will be both physical and digital, with the digital component hosted on the library's website.

I am particularly interested in the way that textile traditions are passed down through families and communities, and how these traditions adapt when people migrate to a new country. Darebin is home to significant communities from the Indian subcontinent, Southeast Asia, the Horn of Africa, and the Balkans, among others. I hope the project will surface stories that are not often represented in mainstream arts programming.

**Workshop structure:**
I will run ten fortnightly documentation sessions, each with a maximum of eight participants. Each session will follow a similar structure:
- Welcome and introduction to the project (15 minutes)
- Individual documentation: photographing and recording the story of each participant's textile object (45 minutes)
- Group discussion and tea (30 minutes)
- Optional: guided embroidery activity where participants can begin a small response piece (30 minutes)

Sessions will be held on Saturday afternoons in the library's meeting room, which I understand is bookable through the standard community room booking process. I will also offer one evening session per month for those who work on weekends.

**Section 4: Project Proposal Summary**

Project title: The Cloth That Remembers: A Community Textile Archive

Project summary (50 words):
A community archive of personal textile objects and their stories, created through ten fortnightly documentation sessions at the library. Participants bring a meaningful textile item, have it photographed, share its story, and receive a small embroidered response piece. The archive will be displayed physically and hosted digitally on the library website.

Project description (full):

*Background:*

The idea for this project came from conversations I had with my mother and her friends at the Reservoir library in September 2024. Several of the women mentioned that they had kept small pieces of fabric from their lives in Korea — a scrap from a daughter's wedding dress, a square cut from a grandfather's winter coat, a ribbon from a first child's birth celebration — but that these objects had no context for their Australian-born grandchildren. One woman said, "When I die, these pieces will go in the bin because no one will know what they mean."

This is not a problem unique to the Korean community. In my work in Seoul, I have run similar documentation projects with migrant communities from Vietnam, the Philippines, and Nepal, and the same pattern emerges: textiles are kept, but their stories are not passed on. The objects survive; the narratives do not.

This project will document the textile objects — quilts, embroidered cloths, baby wraps, ceremonial garments, and everyday mending — that Korean migrants have brought to Australia or made here. Over six months, I will run a series of small-group documentation sessions where participants can bring an object, tell its story, and have both photographed and audio-recorded. 2. Who will participate in the project, and how will they be involved?

The primary participants will be Korean migrants aged 60 and over who live in

participants will show their textile objects, tell the stories behind them,

included in the exhibition. Participants will also be invited to attend the
exhibition opening and to contribute to a short printed catalogue if they

3. Describe the activities you will undertake.

a. February 2025 — Recruitment and planning. I will finalise the session

      portable light box, a digital camera, and an audio recorder. With

      discussion.

      recordings, prepare draft narratives, and meet individually with
      participants to review their stories and photographs. Revisions will

   d. June 2025 — Exhibition design and installation. I will select and print
      photographs, write wall texts in English and Korean, and work with
      library staff to install the exhibition.

      display at Preston Library for the month of July, with a public opening
      event and a closing thank-you gathering for participants.

Folk Museum of Korea in Seoul, where I ran hands-on programmes for older
adults, including textile and craft workshops. Since moving to Australia in
2023, I have volunteered at Darebin Libraries' English conversation group
and have assisted with two multicultural community events at Preston
Library. I have a Bachelor of Fine Arts from Hongik University and a
Graduate Diploma in Community Cultural Development from RMIT (completed

can prepare bilingual materials in Korean and English.

The project will preserve a part of Darebin's Korean migrant heritage that
is currently held privately in people's homes and is at risk of being lost.

residents understand the migration experiences of their neighbours, and it
will give older Korean residents a sense that their histories are valued by
